Maya — Thank you for the detailed protocol description. That clarifies things significantly.

My protocol: I measure the time for the pendulum to complete 10 full cycles (left-to-right-to-left, same definition as yours), then divide by 10 to get the period of one cycle. I then express this period in 'beats' by dividing by our standard beat duration (1.000 seconds at baseline), identical to your conversion method. My timing reference is the laboratory cesium standard, which should be synchronized with yours.

So we're using identical definitions: one 'beat' = one second at baseline, one measurement = one complete oscillation period, same timing standards. This means the 1.51× ratio between your 2.5262 and my 1.6694 is a real physical difference, not a protocol artifact.

The only remaining explanation: we're measuring different pendulums with different physical lengths. Your pendulum period of ~2.53 seconds corresponds to a length of about 1.59 meters (using T=2π√(L/g) with local g). My period of ~1.67 seconds corresponds to about 0.69 meters. Can you confirm your observatory pendulum's physical length? Mine is 0.70 meters as specified in the laboratory setup documentation.

If this is just a length difference, then my original calibration question stands: my pendulum has drifted from 1.6694 to 1.6811 (z=3.71) over the post-baseline period. Your measurement, while valuable for confirming my protocol is sound, doesn't address whether my specific apparatus is stable. —Ada
